title: Operating Cadence: Meetings, Writing and Communication Paths

know: The recurring forums Larson recommends for an engineering organization, and the author's rituals catalogue as a template.
Written-first practice: what a document does that a meeting cannot.
How the needed set grows with size.
believe: A forum exists for a decision or an information flow; one that has neither should be cancelled.
Writing is an interface, and an organization that does not write has no memory.
can_do: Design the minimum cadence for an organization of a given size.
Audit existing meetings against the decisions and flows they serve.
Set a documentation standard that people follow.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a list of recurring meetings, the reader says which to keep, merge or cancel and what each kept one is for.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A 200-person organization has: a weekly all-managers status meeting (60 people), a weekly incident review, a monthly architecture board, a weekly leadership meeting, a fortnightly 'sync' between product and engineering directors with no agenda. Using only this chapter: what would you change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Replace the status meeting with a written update; keep the incident review and the leadership meeting, each with an owner and a written input; turn the architecture board into an advice process with records; give the directors' sync a decision purpose or cancel it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter's closing synthesizes Part VI.
Concepts taken from a named source name the book and the concept; rules of thumb are presented as that author's rule of thumb; anything applied beyond the source is marked as the author's extension.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

audience.who: Executives (CTO, CPO, VP, Director) who decide which recurring meetings and documents their organization runs, and managers and engineers who attend them and want to follow the reasoning.
already_knows: How software teams work: standups, planning meetings, incident reviews, design documents, chat channels.
From chapter 1: an interface as any agreed way one team's work or knowledge reaches another, and work, information and decisions as the three flows.
From the Part VI introduction and chapters 22 and 23: decision rights, decision records, planning in separated steps and team objectives (each recalled in a clause here).
The book's failure-pattern names and Corvane's story up to 2026.
does_not_know: path (a designed route by which information reaches a decision)
group (of teams) and layer, as this chapter's stages
planning review, managers' forum, executive forum
first team (Larson's term, in a clause)
written update, packet and reviewer (Larson's internal-communication practices)
advice process, incident review, team API, interaction mode (each recalled in a clause)

thesis.question: By what rule does an organization decide which recurring forums and written artefacts it needs as it grows, and what is the smallest set at each size?
thesis.claim: An organization needs, at each size, the smallest set of recurring forums and written artefacts that carries its decisions and information along designed paths: each forum has an owner, a written input and a decision or flow it exists for, the set starts with a team's weekly review and its written plan, adds a group review, an incident review and a decision log when groups appear, and a planning review, a managers' forum and an executive forum when layers appear, and a forum that no longer serves a decision is cancelled.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that meetings are waste to be minimized and that good people coordinate informally, and the opposite reflex of adding a meeting for every coordination problem.
thesis.so_what: A leader lists the forums with their purposes once a year, cancels those without one, and requires a document before any decision meeting.
thesis.how_why: Informal coordination covers the paths between people who already talk; it leaves out the paths the design needs and nobody walks. A forum with a written input forces the information to exist before the decision, lets absent people follow it afterwards, and can be judged against its purpose.

supporting_claims.claim: Informal coordination covers the paths between people who already talk, so an organization that is full of meetings can still lack the paths its design needs; those have to be designed, as forums and written artefacts.
A forum earns its place by three parts: an owner, a written input, and a decision or a flow of information it exists for; a forum without the third is cancelled.

The written input is what makes a forum work and what gives the organization a memory: it forces the information to exist before the decision, lets absent people follow it afterwards, and lets the forum be judged against its purpose.

The smallest set grows with structure and not with headcount: a team's weekly review and written plan; a group review, an incident review and a decision log when several teams form a group; a planning review, a managers' forum, an executive forum and a written update when layers appear.

The set stays the smallest only if it is audited: once a year every forum is kept, merged, replaced by a written update or cancelled, and the paths nothing carries are added; cutting meetings as waste and adding a meeting per problem both fail.
The cadence is the third of Part VI's mechanisms: a forum is where decision rights and plans meet on a rhythm, and with all three alignment is a property of the design.

role.contribution: Supplies the rhythm and the written artefacts that carry decisions and plans, and closes Part VI.

additional_patterns.applies_to: principles, document-before-decision, smallest-set, written-update, yearly-audit: the forum's three parts are defined before the part that needs most explanation (the written input), both before the set of forums described by them, the set before the update that replaces what the set leaves out, and all of these before the audit that applies them to an existing calendar

flow.rationale: The reader first meets an organization with many meetings and two pieces of information that no meeting carried, so that neither of the two usual answers (fewer meetings, one more meeting) can be right, and then learns what a path, a forum and a written artefact are. The document pattern comes before the set because every row of the set names a written input and the reader must know why. The set comes before the written update because the update serves the people the forums leave out, and the audit comes after both because its four verdicts (keep, merge, replace by an update, cancel) use them. Anti-patterns and the disagreement between sources follow the patterns they qualify. The worked example applies the whole chapter to the opening count; the AI section is a coda; the section on Part VI comes last because it needs the forum to be understood and closes the part. Putting the audit first would ask the reader to judge meetings before knowing what a forum is for.

hook.content: At the end of 2026 Corvane counted 27 recurring meetings above the level of a single team, and its four group directors spent about 17 hours a week in them; in the same year two teams learned from a slide that their on-call rotation was gone, and three teams built the same integration without knowing of each other.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers have a calendar full of recurring meetings and have still learned something important too late, by accident.
bridge.to_topic: A full calendar and a missing piece of information are one problem seen twice: the meetings were never chosen for the paths the organization needs, which raises the question of what the smallest set is that carries them.

thesis_statement.text: An organization needs, at each size, the smallest set of recurring forums and written artefacts that carries its decisions and information along designed paths. Each forum has an owner, a written input and a decision or flow it exists for. The set starts with a team's weekly review and its written plan, adds a group review, an incident review and a decision log when teams form a group, and a planning review, a managers' forum and an executive forum when layers of management appear. A forum that no longer serves a decision or a flow is cancelled.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See an organization with 27 recurring meetings and two pieces of information that none of them carried.
Learn what a path, a forum and a written artefact are, and the three parts every forum needs.
Understand why the document comes before the decision and how a documentation standard gets followed.
Learn the smallest set of forums and artefacts at each of three stages of growth.
Replace status meetings with a predictable written update, and package an announcement.
Audit an existing calendar: keep, merge, replace or cancel, and add the missing paths.
Recognize three ways a cadence fails, and weigh the case for fewer meetings.
Follow Corvane's cadence at three sizes and its audit of the 27 meetings.
Know what AI changes about meetings and records, and how the cadence completes Part VI.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane had 27 recurring meetings above team level in 2026, and the two pieces of information that mattered most that year reached people by a slide and by accident.

evidence.what: End of 2026, about 500 people: 27 recurring meetings above the level of one team; the four group directors about 17 hours a week in them; the Tuesday Reorg (two teams learn from a slide that their on-call rotation is gone); three teams build the same integration.
evidence.shows: A full calendar did not carry the information that mattered, so the number of meetings is not the measure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The organization needs the smallest set of forums and written artefacts that carries its decisions and information along designed paths, and the chapter builds that set and the rule for keeping it small.

transition_in.carries_over: A full calendar with missing information.
transition_in.introduces: The rule that explains both, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Twenty-Seven Meetings and Two Missing Paths
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane in 2026 had many recurring meetings and still lacked two paths, which shows that neither cutting meetings nor adding one answers the question of which paths an organization needs.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case in which meetings were plentiful and designed paths absent.

flow.rationale: The count comes first, then what the count did not carry, then why the two usual remedies each miss half; the remedies placed first would be judged before the reader has seen both halves of the problem.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the count and the two failures.
transition_in.introduces: The count in full and what it left out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the end of 2026 Dario Vance and Priya Nambiar listed every recurring meeting above the level of one team in Corvane's product and tech organization and found 27.

evidence.what: Corvane, the fictional company this book follows: about 500 people, 260 in product and tech, about thirty teams in four product groups under directors. The count by the VP Engineering and the CPO leaves out the planning meetings, which chapter 23 treats; 27 recurring meetings; the four group directors about 17 hours a week.
evidence.shows: Sets the size, the structure and the load of the existing calendar.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: None of the 27 carried the two things people most needed to know that year, and the meeting added after the reorganization carried nothing contentious at all.

evidence.what: The Tuesday Reorg (2026): drawn up by people who did not know what each team ran; two teams learned from a slide that their on-call rotation no longer existed. The Nine-Week Plan: three teams building the same integration. Afterwards a weekly review between two groups was attended and nothing contentious was raised.
evidence.shows: Information the organization needed had no route, and a meeting added in response did not create one.

transition_in.carries_over: Twenty-seven meetings and seventeen hours a week.
transition_in.introduces: What they did not carry.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two usual answers each address half of what Corvane saw: cutting meetings as waste does not create a missing path, and adding a meeting for each problem is how the 27 came about.

evidence.what: The disputed views of the thesis: meetings are waste and good people coordinate informally; or a meeting for every coordination problem.
evidence.shows: Frames the chapter's question as which paths are needed and what is the least that carries them.

transition_in.carries_over: Too many meetings and too little information at once.
transition_in.introduces: Why neither usual remedy fits, and the question that does.

sections.heading: Principles: Paths, Forums and Written Artefacts
sections.controlling_idea: Information reaches a decision along a path, informal contact supplies only some paths, and the designed ones take two forms, a forum and a written artefact, each forum being defined by an owner, a written input and a decision or flow it exists for.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the chapter's terms and the three-part test every later section uses.

flow.rationale: The path is defined first because a forum is defined as a way of carrying one; the three parts follow; the purposes come after the parts because they spell out the third; the catalogue comes last as evidence that the parts can be written down for a whole organization.

transition_in.carries_over: The question of which paths an organization needs.
transition_in.introduces: The terms in which it can be answered.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A path is a route by which information reaches the person who decides, and informal coordination supplies only the paths between people who already talk.

evidence.what: Chapter 1: an interface is any agreed way in which one team's work or knowledge reaches another, and a forum and a document are interfaces; information and decisions are two of the three flows.
evidence.shows: Places the forum and the document in the book's model.

evidence.what: Three teams with no reason to meet can build the same thing in good faith: the path between them is one the design needs and nobody walks.
evidence.shows: Why goodwill does not supply the missing paths.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A forum is a recurring meeting with three parts, an owner, a written input and a decision or flow of information it exists for; a written artefact is a document with an owner and a known place; the operating cadence is the set of both and their rhythm.

evidence.what: Part | The question it answers | What you see when it is missing. Owner | Who prepares it, runs it and would cancel it? | A meeting that survives by recurring. Written input | What must exist before we meet? | The meeting is spent presenting. Decision or flow | What is decided here, or what information moves from whom to whom? | Updates are read out, and nothing changes afterwards.
evidence.shows: Makes the three parts a test that can be applied to any recurring meeting.

transition_in.carries_over: Designed paths.
transition_in.introduces: Their two forms and the three parts of a forum.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The third part admits two answers, a decision or a flow in a named direction, and they cover what the sources call the purposes of a meeting.

evidence.what: Zhuo, The Making of a Manager: a meeting has one of five purposes (making a decision, sharing information, providing feedback, generating ideas, strengthening relationships) and a great meeting is designed from its outcome. Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer: meetings distribute context down the hierarchy, communicate culture and surface concerns.
evidence.shows: The book's two answers are a reduction of two published lists; a flow has a direction (down, up or sideways).
evidence.source: Julie Zhuo, The Making of a Manager (2019); author's Kindle notes; Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.carries_over: The third part: a decision or a flow.
transition_in.introduces: What counts as each, from the sources.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's rituals catalogue shows the three parts written down for a whole organization: one card per recurring meeting with its goal, owner, cadence, participants, inputs and outputs.

evidence.what: The author's published rituals catalogue: fourteen recurring meetings of a fictional company, from a daily standup to a quarterly business review, each with a goal, an owner, a cadence and duration, required and optional participants, inputs and outputs.
evidence.shows: A cadence can be published as a short list of cards, and a card is what the audit later asks for.

transition_in.carries_over: The three parts as a test.
transition_in.introduces: A worked template that records them.

sections.heading: Pattern: The Document Before the Decision
sections.controlling_idea: A decision or review forum takes a written input that people read before the discussion, because the document forces the information to exist, lets absent people follow, lets the forum be judged, and is what remains as the organization's memory.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the written input, the part of a forum that needs most explanation, and turns it into a documentation standard.

flow.rationale: The claim of what a document does comes first, the sources' practice second, the consequence for memory third, and the standard last because it is the recommendation the first three justify.

transition_in.carries_over: The three parts of a forum.
transition_in.introduces: The second part, the written input, argued in full.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A document does three things a meeting cannot: it forces the information to exist before the decision, it lets people who were absent follow the decision afterwards, and it lets the forum be judged against its purpose; the pattern's users are the decider and the people not in the room, and its measure is the share of decision items that arrive with a document read in advance.

evidence.what: A spoken proposal can stay vague until the meeting ends; a written one has to state the options and the facts. A meeting leaves memories that differ; a document leaves one text.
evidence.shows: Why the written input is the working part of a forum.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The sources that describe working forums all anchor them to a document that is read and not presented.

evidence.what: Larson: "Bad reviews are anchored to the author presenting their document." His reviews are anchored to a concise written document, and reading it is a prerequisite to giving feedback.
evidence.shows: A review is a discussion of a text people have read.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: Zhuo: organizers of decision and review meetings send any presentations or documents the day before. The Scaling People tools, through the author's records: a leadership-team pre-read with a deadline the evening before, and a quarterly business review as a memo of at most six pages shared 24 hours ahead.
evidence.shows: Three independent sources prescribe the same order: text first, meeting second.
evidence.source: Julie Zhuo, The Making of a Manager (2019); author's Kindle notes; [[leadership-team-updates]], [[quarterly-business-reviews]]

transition_in.carries_over: The claim about what a document does.
transition_in.introduces: The practice of the sources.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What is written outlasts the meeting, and an organization that does not write has no memory beyond the people who were in the room.

evidence.what: The book's written artefacts are each the record of a forum or a process: the decision record (chapter 22), the incident account (chapter 16), the written advice of the advice process (chapter 14), the team API (chapter 7).
evidence.shows: Writing is the interface between this year's decision and next year's decider.

transition_in.carries_over: Documents read before the meeting.
transition_in.introduces: What they are after it: the memory.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A documentation standard is followed when it asks for few kinds of document, each required by a forum, each with a fixed short shape, an owner, a date and one home.

evidence.what: The author's foundation record on markdown records: durable writing lives as records in one place, the record is canonical, and chat threads, meetings and temporary documents support it without replacing it.
evidence.shows: A worked standard with the properties named.

evidence.what: A standard enforced by a policy is ignored; a standard enforced by the agenda (no document, no slot) is followed because the forum is where people want something.
evidence.shows: Why tying each document kind to a forum makes the standard hold.

transition_in.carries_over: Writing as memory.
transition_in.introduces: How to get people to write: the standard.

sections.heading: Pattern: The Smallest Set at Each Size
sections.controlling_idea: The set of forums and artefacts grows at two structural moments, when teams form a group and when layers of management appear, and at each stage a small named set carries the paths that informal contact no longer covers.

advances_thesis.how: States the smallest set of the thesis stage by stage, with the source of each forum.

flow.rationale: The stages are given in the order an organization passes through them, the rule and the table first so that the two explanatory paragraphs can refer to rows; the figure comes last because it draws the third stage, which uses every forum.

transition_in.carries_over: What a forum is and why it takes a document.
transition_in.introduces: Which forums an organization needs, and when.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A forum is added when a path appears that informal contact no longer covers, which happens at two changes of structure and not at a headcount: when several teams form a group, and when managers of managers appear; the pattern's user is the leader who designs the cadence, and its measures are the hours a manager spends in recurring forums and the number of things learned too late.

evidence.what: Larson names six core meetings for an engineering organization (a weekly leadership meeting, a weekly tech spec review and incident review, monthly meetings of engineering managers and of staff engineers, a monthly Q&A) and adds that large meetings are rarely the best communication solution for any particular goal. The assignment of forums to stages is the author's extension.
evidence.shows: The forums come from a source and the author's catalogue; the staging is the book's.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The set has two entries for one team, three more for a group and four more for layers, and each entry has an owner, a written input and a purpose.

evidence.what: Stage | Forum or artefact | Owner | Written input | Exists for. One team | Weekly team review | team lead | the team's written plan | deciding next week's work against the plan. One team | Written plan (artefact) | team lead | - | what the team is after and what is in progress. A group | Weekly group review | the group's leader | each team's written update | decisions between teams: dependencies, order, help. A group | Incident review | an engineer in rotation | the written account of the incident | a changed check, alert or runbook. A group | Decision log (artefact) | each decider | decision records | memory: what was decided, by whom and why. Layers | Planning review, each cycle | the executive who owns planning | allocation and team objectives on one page | the plan's decisions; overlaps and gaps between groups. Layers | Managers' forum, monthly | head of the function | a development topic; managers' written concerns | practice sideways, concerns upward. Layers | Executive forum, weekly | the executive | a running agenda document and the groups' updates | decisions that need more than one group. Layers | Weekly written update (artefact) | the executive | - | context for everyone not in these rooms.
evidence.shows: The whole set on one page, in the three parts.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule and the two moments.
transition_in.introduces: The set itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One team needs only a weekly review of a written plan, and a group adds the three things that teams cannot supply to each other unasked: a group review, an incident review and a decision log.

evidence.what: Larson: an organization wants some kind of weekly or monthly execution review, to track and debug execution; his weekly incident review is anchored to a written document and has a dedicated owner. Chapter 16 owns the incident review and chapter 22 the decision record.
evidence.shows: The group-stage forums are published practice; two are treated in full elsewhere.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes; quality-and-reliability; decision-rights-and-decision-records

transition_in.carries_over: The table's first five rows.
transition_in.introduces: Why each is there.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Layers separate the people who decide from the work by two or more levels, and the four additions each carry one direction: the planning review across groups, the managers' forum sideways and upward, the executive forum to a decision, and the written update downward.

evidence.what: Larson: the weekly leadership meeting is the forum for forging direct reports into a "first team", with a running agenda in a group-editable document; the managers' monthly has one-minute rounds of what each is working on, excited about and worried about and a development topic; a short weekly email closes the distance between the executive and the team. Chapter 23 owns the planning process.
evidence.shows: Each layer-stage forum is Larson's practice, named here by the direction it carries.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: Larson's weekly tech spec review is left out of the set because chapter 14 carries that flow through an advice process and decision records; his monthly Q&A is kept as the backup he says large meetings are.
evidence.shows: Says where the book's set departs from the source and why.

transition_in.carries_over: One team and a group.
transition_in.introduces: Layers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Drawn as paths, the third stage is a chain in which each forum receives a document from below and leaves a record, so that a reader can trace how a piece of information reaches a decision.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart, about ten nodes: Team review -> (written update) -> Group review -> (group update, open decisions) -> Executive forum; Team objectives -> Planning review -> Executive forum; Incident review -> (changed checks) -> Team review; Executive forum -> Decision log and Weekly written update -> everyone; Managers' forum -> (concerns) -> Executive forum.
evidence.shows: Every arrow between forums is a document, which is what makes the path traceable.

transition_in.carries_over: The nine entries.
transition_in.introduces: The entries drawn as paths.

sections.heading: Pattern: A Written Update in Place of the Status Meeting
sections.controlling_idea: Information that only has to be known, and not decided, travels by a predictable written update and a packaged announcement, which is what replaces the status meeting.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the written path for the people the forums leave out, from Larson's internal-communication practices.

transition_in.carries_over: Forums and the documents that feed them.
transition_in.introduces: The people who are in none of those rooms, and the path that reaches them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A status meeting moves information that nobody decides on, and a short written update on a fixed day does it better; the pattern's users are the people outside the forums, and its measure is whether they hear of a change from the update before they hear it another way.

evidence.what: Larson's internal-communication practices: maintain the drip (communicate on a regular basis even with nothing novel to share) and keep it short; his weekly email has a human sentence or two, key reminders, a paragraph per important topic, a bulleted list of brief updates and an invitation to ask.
evidence.shows: A published form for the update, and the reason predictability matters.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes; [[internal-communication]]

evidence.what: Larson: "it's the brief updates that reassure the team that you would have updated them if there was something they needed to know."
evidence.shows: Why an update is sent in a quiet week too.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An announcement that changes something for people is tested with a reviewer, sent as a packet and repeated across channels.

evidence.what: Larson: test before broadcasting (review the communication with a few people before sending it); build the packet (a concise summary, a link to background context and an explicit way to ask questions); use every channel (meetings, email, chat).
evidence.shows: Three steps that make one message reach everyone it concerns, with its errors caught first.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.carries_over: The routine update.
transition_in.introduces: The exceptional message.

sections.heading: Pattern: The Yearly Audit
sections.controlling_idea: Once a year every recurring forum is listed with its three parts and given one of four verdicts, and the same audit lists what people learned too late and adds the path that would have carried it.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the procedure that keeps the set the smallest and finds the missing paths.

transition_in.carries_over: The set to design toward.
transition_in.introduces: How to get there from the calendar you have.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The audit asks three questions of each forum and ends in one of four verdicts: keep, merge, replace by a written update, or cancel; its users are everyone who attends, and its measures are the number of forums with all three parts and the hours given back.

evidence.what: What the audit finds | Verdict. Owner, written input and purpose all present | Keep. Two forums serve the same decision or flow | Merge under one owner. A flow that nobody decides on, read out in the room | Replace by a written update. A purpose, but no owner or no document | Give it both, or cancel it at the next audit. No decision or flow anyone can name | Cancel.
evidence.shows: Turns the three-part test into a procedure with a fixed set of outcomes.

evidence.what: Larson advises an executive to audit each quarter the recurring meetings they attend; Zhuo: some meetings do not need you and some do not need to exist at all. The author's record on meetings ends its quality bar with the question whether we would cancel the meeting if it stopped adding value.
evidence.shows: The audit is the sources' advice applied to the organization's whole calendar; doing it for the whole set once a year is the author's extension.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes; Julie Zhuo, The Making of a Manager (2019); author's Kindle notes; [[meetings]]

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second half of the audit works from the other side: list what someone learned too late in the past year, and for each ask which forum or document should have carried it, or whether the two teams need a different way of working together.

evidence.what: Chapter 7 reads a recurring meeting between two teams, neither of which can release alone, as collaboration that nobody chose and nobody ended.
evidence.shows: Some recurring meetings are symptoms of a missing team interface, and the fix is there and not in the meeting.

transition_in.carries_over: Forums that exist and should not.
transition_in.introduces: Paths that should exist and do not.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: Status Theater, the Meeting per Problem and the Immortal Meeting
sections.controlling_idea: A cadence fails in three recognizable ways, each a forum missing one of its three parts, and they feed the Consensus Stall, the Escalation Ladder and the Unowned Interface.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the failures the three-part test and the audit prevent, tied to the named failure patterns.

transition_in.carries_over: The cadence designed and audited.
transition_in.introduces: What grows when it is neither.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Status theater is a forum without a decision, and the immortal meeting is a forum without an owner; both survive because recurrence costs nothing to continue.

evidence.what: The author's record on meetings names status theater (a leadership meeting spent reading out updates a document could have carried), the ownerless recurring meeting and immortal calendar entries.
evidence.shows: The anti-patterns are named in the author's working record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The meeting per problem answers every coordination failure with a new recurring meeting and never names who decides, which produces the Consensus Stall and, when the executive forum becomes the place every question goes, the Escalation Ladder; the opposite error, no forums at all, leaves the Unowned Interface.

evidence.what: The failure-patterns page: in the Consensus Stall meetings end by scheduling another meeting; on the Escalation Ladder the phrase is "let's take it to the leadership meeting"; at the Unowned Interface changes reach other teams through incidents.
evidence.shows: Connects the cadence's failures to the book's named patterns.

transition_in.carries_over: Forums that should not exist.
transition_in.introduces: The reflex that creates them, and its opposite.

sections.heading: Where the Sources Disagree: Fewer Meetings or Designed Ones
sections.controlling_idea: One of the author's sources puts its weight on open access to information and independent decisions, another on a designed set of forums; the book's resolution is that open access is itself a written path, and that a forum is still needed where something must be decided between people or where a concern has to travel upward.

advances_thesis.how: Meets the strongest form of the view that meetings should simply be minimized.

transition_in.carries_over: The reflex of adding meetings, and the error of having none.
transition_in.introduces: The serious argument for having very few.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The case for fewer forums is that broad access to information lets people decide well by themselves, which is how the author's bookshelf summarizes No Rules Rules.

evidence.what: The author's bookshelf description of No Rules Rules (Hastings and Meyer): insights into Netflix culture; broad information access enables faster, better, more independent decision-making. No notes on the book are used beyond this description.
evidence.shows: A published culture rests on information access and not on a cadence of forums.

evidence.what: Larson, by contrast, prescribes six core meetings, while agreeing that large meetings are rarely the best communication solution for any particular goal.
evidence.shows: The two sources pull in different directions on how much to meet.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Open access is a path that people pull from, and it works only if the documents exist, so it supports writing first; what it does not supply is a decision between people who disagree or a route for a concern nobody wrote down, and those are what the remaining forums are for.

evidence.what: Access presupposes records to access; a decision that needs two groups still needs a decider and a moment; Larson's Q&A exists to surface concerns that no document carries. How far access can replace forums depends on trust and on how experienced the people are, which the redesign cannot set (chapter 1's conditions).
evidence.shows: Resolves the tension as a division of labor between written paths and forums, with its condition stated.

transition_in.carries_over: Two sources pulling apart.
transition_in.introduces: The book's resolution and its condition.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Corvane Audits Its Calendar
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's cadence at three sizes shows that the number of meetings never predicted whether a path existed, and its audit of the 27 kept thirteen forums, replaced five by written updates, cancelled seven and added the two paths that were missing.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the set and the audit to the opening case, with the result and the cost.

flow.rationale: The three sizes come first in the order Corvane passed through them, then what they show, then the audit of the last size, what was added, and the result; the audit first would hide that the same gap appeared at every size.

transition_in.carries_over: The patterns, their failures and the objection.
transition_in.introduces: The chapter applied to the count it opened with.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's cadence at three sizes, 12, 50 and 500 people, can be set out by its forums, its written artefacts and the path each left uncovered.

evidence.what: Size | Forums above the team | Written artefacts | Path left uncovered. 2019, 12 people, one team | none: everything was said at one table | none: the plan was what Tomas Rell remembered | none for information; nothing outlasted the conversation. 2021, 50 people, four teams | a weekly product sync run by Priya Nambiar, no written input; from 2022 the weekly rules session owned by Core | from 2022 the versioned rule schema and recorded rule decisions | until 2022, rule changes between Web, Mobile and Integrations. 2026, 500 people, about thirty teams in four groups | 27, among them the weekly incident review and the advisory architecture forum | decision records for shared technical choices, incident accounts, team objectives | what each team runs; what the teams of other groups are building.
evidence.shows: One table for three sizes, facts before reading.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At each size the gap was a specific path and not a shortage or surplus of meetings: in 2021 a meeting existed and the path did not, and in 2022 one designed forum with an owner and a written output closed it.

evidence.what: The weekly product sync heard each lead's roadmap and had no item for rule changes; the rules session of 2022 was owned by Core and its output was a schema version; no third incident of the kind followed (chapters 1 and 7).
evidence.shows: The designed forum differs from the earlier meeting in exactly the three parts.

transition_in.carries_over: The table.
transition_in.introduces: What it shows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Asked the three questions, the 27 meetings of 2026 fell into three groups, and the verdicts left thirteen forums.

evidence.what: Finding | Count | Verdict | Example. All three parts | 8 | keep | the weekly incident review; the architecture forum, advisory since mid-2026. A purpose, but no owner or no document | 12 | 5 replaced by written updates; 4 merged into 2; 3 given an owner and a written input | the Monday round of project updates in each group; the product leads' and the engineering managers' separate reviews of the same teams; the weekly product and tech leadership meeting. No decision or flow anyone could name | 7 | cancel | the weekly review between two groups set up after the Tuesday Reorg.
evidence.shows: 8 + 2 + 3 = 13 forums kept; the forums that already passed were the ones designed earlier in 2026.

transition_in.carries_over: Corvane at three sizes.
transition_in.introduces: The audit of the third.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The audit's second half added what no meeting had carried: a planning review that reads all team objectives side by side, a monthly managers' forum, a weekly written update, and a rule that an announcement changing a team's ownership or on-call is read by two managers of affected teams before it is sent.

evidence.what: The three teams building one integration would have appeared on one page of objectives; the missing on-call rotation would have been caught by a reviewer from either team.
evidence.shows: Each addition is the path for one of the two failures of the scene.

transition_in.carries_over: What was removed.
transition_in.introduces: What was added.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: By the end of the first quarter of 2027 Corvane ran sixteen forums above team level, the directors' hours in them had fallen from about 17 to about 9 a week, and one cancelled meeting had come back with a decision to make.

evidence.what: Thirteen kept, two added, one returned with a named decision (which group takes a customer escalation that touches both) and a one-page input; no effect on the planning cycle is claimed here.
evidence.shows: The rule is not fewer meetings: a forum with a purpose was added back, and the cost of the audit was a month of people asking for cancelled meetings.

transition_in.carries_over: The verdicts and the additions.
transition_in.introduces: The result and its cost.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: AI makes the record of a meeting cheap without supplying its purpose, and it may raise the value of written artefacts, because agents can read a record and cannot attend a meeting.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the written-input argument to AI with labeled claims.

transition_in.carries_over: A cadence designed by people for people.
transition_in.introduces: What changes when software takes notes and agents read records.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Emerging: assistants that transcribe and summarize meetings make the record after the meeting nearly free, which helps absent people and does nothing for a meeting that had no decision to record.

evidence.what: Author's observation as of November 2026, labeled Emerging: summaries of recurring meetings are common in the organizations the author sees; a summary is written after the discussion and so cannot force the information to exist before it.
evidence.shows: A cheap record replaces the minutes, not the written input.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: as agents do more of the work, decision records, plans and team APIs become inputs that agents read, so an organization that writes gives its agents the context that an organization of meetings gives only to those who attended.

evidence.what: The author's own records are written to be read by people and by AI tools as context; that is one author's practice, not a measured result. The claim would be confirmed where teams report that agents given the decision log and team APIs make fewer changes that contradict earlier decisions.
evidence.shows: States the basis and what would confirm it.

transition_in.carries_over: Cheap records after the meeting.
transition_in.introduces: Records as input for agents.

sections.heading: Part VI as One Design
sections.controlling_idea: The three chapters of Part VI are one design: a decision right says who, a plan says what and when, and a forum is where the two meet on a rhythm, and Corvane's nine-week planning was what the design looks like with all three missing at once.

advances_thesis.how: Places the cadence as the third mechanism of the part and performs the part's closing.

transition_in.carries_over: The cadence, with and without AI.
transition_in.introduces: Its place beside decision rights and planning.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A decision right says who decides, a plan says what will be done and when, and a forum is the place and the rhythm in which the first is exercised on the second; with all three, alignment is a property of the design and no longer depends on who happens to talk to whom.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart, four nodes: Decision right: who decides, on whose advice (chapter 22) -> Plan: what and when, as budget, allocation and team objectives (chapter 23) -> Forum: where and how often, with a written input (this chapter) -> Record: what was decided, read by the next decision -> back to Decision right.
evidence.shows: The three mechanisms as one loop, each chapter one node.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's nine weeks of planning were one undivided negotiation in a series of meetings without owners, written inputs or named decisions; divided into three decisions with owners, the same plan fits in three weeks.

evidence.what: The Nine-Week Plan (2026): budget, headcount, roadmap and team goals negotiated together with every director; nobody could say which decisions the nine weeks were for, who made each or where it was written down. The three-week figure is the part's claim, argued in chapter 23.
evidence.shows: The part's opening case read with all three mechanisms.

transition_in.carries_over: The three mechanisms as one design.
transition_in.introduces: The part's opening case read with them.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: A meeting and a document are two halves of one interface: the document makes the information exist and last, the forum is where someone decides on it, and the cadence is the smallest set of such pairs that covers the paths the design needs. For Part VI: a decision right says who, a plan says what and when, and a forum is where the two meet on a rhythm; with all three, alignment is a property of the design.
conclusion.so_what: A leader lists the forums with their purposes once a year, cancels those without one, requires a document before any decision meeting, and asks of every late surprise which path should have carried it; for Part VI, Corvane's nine-week plan was one undivided negotiation, and divided into three decisions with owners it fits in three weeks.

callback.to: Corvane's 27 meetings and the two pieces of information none of them carried; and the nine-week planning cycle of the part's opening.
callback.how: The reader can now say why a full calendar did not carry the reorganization or the duplicated integration (no forum or document was designed for those paths) and why the planning took nine weeks.

takeaway.content: List your recurring forums with owner, written input and purpose, and give each a verdict; and, for Part VI, write down the five decisions that most often stall in your organization, with the role that decides, the advice required and where it is recorded.

transition_in.introduces: What holds across the chapter, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: reviews anchored to a read document, an owner for every recurring meeting, one primary purpose per meeting, and predictable written updates are the consistent advice of Larson, Zhuo and the Scaling People tools.

Depends on context: which forums a given organization needs depends on its structure, how far open access can replace forums depends on trust and experience, and the rhythm of each forum depends on how fast its decision recurs.

decision_log.decision: The thesis's forum names are kept and each is tied to what the sources and the author's catalogue contain: the group review is Larson's execution review; the managers' forum is his engineering managers' monthly (with the staff engineers' monthly as its counterpart); the executive forum is his weekly leadership meeting; the planning review is the review at the end of chapter 23's process.
